dialogues.text: Hello! Welcome to my world.
Excuse me? Where am I...?
You're inside the blockchain, of course.
Block... what?
Blockchain.
Imagine a huge chain made of blocks, like the cubes you see here.
Each block stores important information, like the pages of a huge public book.
What kind of information?
Almost any kind.
But it's usually information about crypto transactions.
Crypto transactions? What's that?
It's users moving different kinds of digital assets around.
Digital assets? Different kinds?
Indeed, there are several kinds of digital assets.
But for now we'll only focus on fungible assets, commonly known as cryptocurrencies (like the network's digital money) and tokens (which can represent other virtual goods).
Fungible? Cryptocurrencies? Tokens? That's a lot of new words all at once...
Alright, let's not get ahead of ourselves.
For now, all you need to know is that some users need everyone to know that their assets (whatever kind they are) have moved from one place to another.
They manage all of this from their Wallet, which is like a virtual purse or wallet where they keep those tokens.
Okay, and how do they plan to let everyone know they've moved something out of their Wallet?
Relax... it's simpler than you think.
Imagine the blockchain as a huge database that everyone has access to.
Okay, but if everyone has access, couldn't anyone just write down that they own loads of those cryptocurrencies?
Oh, you rascal... your question makes a lot of sense, and that's exactly what the blockchain is here to solve.
The idea is that not just anyone can write to that database: there's a way to stop someone from adding data arbitrarily.
Okay, but then how do they write the data down?
It's very simple.
For a validator (the ones in charge of checking everything) to write new data to this special database, they first have to solve a complex math problem.
And how exactly does that help? Couldn't anyone learn to solve math problems and write whatever they want?
Oh, my friend... it's not that easy. We're talking about very complex problems that only the most powerful computers can solve.
Besides, there are lots of machines trying to solve the same problem at the same time, so someone else can beat you to it and write instead of you.
So the data is controlled by whoever has the most powerful computer?
Something like that could happen in smaller databases still in development, but it shouldn't.
If a single person could choose which data gets added, the network would no longer be secure.
That sounds dangerous... Why would I keep my money in my Wallet if one day someone with a really powerful computer could show up and write a 0 in my balance?
I understand your concern, but luckily that can't happen. There are thousands of validators keeping watch.
If someone tries to cheat, the others will reject their block. And this is where you come in! Today you'll be working as a validator.
Me? But I don't know anything about this... And why would I want to do that job?
For the rewards, of course! Every time someone makes a transaction, they include a small tip called a Fee.
As a validator, you decide which transactions go into your block. And the validator keeps those Fees!
Ah... now that I like! So I just put in every transaction I see and get rich, right?
Not so fast! To do your job well you need to know your tools.
First, look at this indicator. This is where all the Fees you earn will add up.
Now look at the wheel.
Transactions will keep appearing, and each one will have a different reward <sprite="ETH_bag" index=0> and size <sprite="gas" index=0>.
Got it... So I just look for the ones that pay the most and put them straight into the block, right?
Careful, don't rush!
You have to find the perfect balance between the space they take up <sprite="gas" index=0> and the Fee they earn you <sprite="ETH_bag" index=0>.
Balance? What do you mean?
Imagine a transaction that takes up 6 units <sprite="gas" index=0> and pays 4 <sprite="ETH_bag" index=0>.
Shortly after, another one appears that takes up only 2 units <sprite="gas" index=0> and pays 3 <sprite="ETH_bag" index=0>. Which one do you prefer?
Ah... of course. With the second one I earn almost the same, but I use up much less of my 20 <sprite="gas" index=0> limit. I could fit in many more small transactions and earn more money overall!
Exactly! That's the secret of a great validator.
You have to find the most profitable combination, always keeping in mind the time available and your space limit.
Every block has a capacity limit.
Today's blocks hold a maximum of 20 units ( <sprite="gas" index=0> ) of space.
So... My goal is to pick the transactions that give me the most profit overall, keeping in mind the maximum space of 20 <sprite="gas" index=0> and the fee they bring.
Exactly! But remember the golden rule: other validators will try to create the block before you.
Pay close attention to this red bar.
It represents the network's time. If it runs out, you'll lose the block and won't be able to validate it.
Got it! I have to be quick before it runs out.
And where can I see how much space I have left for more transactions?
Very good question. Look at this meter right here.
It shows you in real time how much space you've used in your current block, which has a maximum limit of 20 units <sprite="gas" index=0>.
Okay, so I go for maximum profit without going over that space bar and without running out of time.
Yes, and remember, when you're happy with the transactions you've chosen...
...you'll have to press this button to send your block to the network.
So it's not enough to fill the block. If I don't press Validate before time runs out, I'll lose it.
Exactly! Don't wait until the last second.
As soon as you have a profitable block, validate it before another validator beats you to it.
Finally, on this cube you can see how many blocks you have left to validate.
All clear! Space management, time limit, remaining blocks and my total progress.
I'm ready to be a validator!
Let's do this!
